A dollar stablecoin is trading at $0.92. No recovery has been announced. Your $900 laptop is due next month. A stablecoin aims to hold $1.00, but nothing guarantees it. Its price depends on what backs it, whether it can be redeemed, and confidence in the issuer. It may recover, stay low or fall further. A vault adds its own risks on top (smart-contract problems, withdrawal limits, the protocol itself), and it is not an insured bank account.

A stablecoin is not guaranteed to hold a dollar. Check what backs it and whether you can redeem it. Don't borrow to solve a problem your cash already solves, and decide to sell or hold on your needs and your trust in the asset, not on hope of a rebound.

blurb: A 24-year-old in her first full-time job: a thin cushion, an employer match, a depegged stablecoin and a self-imposed crypto allowance.
intro: Maya, 24, first full-time job. Take-home pay $2,900 a month (after tax, before any retirement contribution; assumed gross $3,800). Living costs $2,350 a month. Opening: checking $500, savings $1,000, retirement account $2,200. No crypto. Each month-end, anything over $500 in checking is moved to savings automatically.
name: Maya Chen
plan: Starter fund: $3,300 of liquid cash (checking + savings).
Full cushion: $4,700 (two months of living costs).

Crypto allowance: $200 in total until the cushion reaches $4,700, and the starter fund must still be at least $3,300 after any purchase. Once the cushion is $4,700 or more after a purchase, the $200 limit no longer applies.
Order of operations: Reserve, then free money (employer match), then wallet safety, then optional experiments.
Cash in this story is checking + savings only. The retirement account and the vault are not cash.
